newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firms cheerier in Nov, rates seen on hold.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms cheerier in Nov, rates seen on hold.

text.p: Japan's corporations grew somewhat cheerier about their business prospects in November but remain cautious about the future, according to a closely watched survey by the Bank of Japan released on Wednesday.

The central bank's quarterly corporate survey, known as the "tankan", showed that the diffusion index for big manufacturers -- an important gauge of corporate sentiment -- rose to minus three in November from minus seven in August, when the previous survey was conducted.
The tankan is a key clue to Japan's monetary policy.

The headline figure was mainly in line with expectations. Private economists polled by Reuters had forecast on average that the manufacturers' diffusion index would rise to around minus three, an improvement but still below the level of zero predicted by the firms themselves in August. The economists' forecasts ranged from minus 10 to zero.
The index represents the percentage of firms expecting business to improve minus those who expect it to worsen. The higher the number, the more optimistic the outlook.

Major non-manufacturing companies also grew more optimistic about short-term prospects, with their diffusion index improving to zero from minus four for August. The firms had forecast a November index of minus three in August.

Meanwhile, major companies said they expected their capital spending to rise seven percent in 1996/97, ending next March, after an actual 1.2 percent rise the previous year. That compared with a November forecast of a 6.6 percent increase.

Big manufacturers said they saw a 14.1 percent increase in profits in 1996/97 after a 35.8 percent rise the previous year, while their non-manufacturing colleagues forecast an 8.1 percent rise against 16.4 percent growth in 1995/96.

Economists said the modest improvement in corporate sentiment was unlikely to prompt the Bank of Japan to tighten interest rates, which it has kept at rock-bottom levels since September 1995, when it slashed its official discount rate to a record low 0.5 percent.

Monetary policy will remain unchanged until about next summer at the earliest, said Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at CS First Boston in Tokyo. "Policy will remain unchanged...not because of the real economy per se, but because of financial sector weakness."

Big Japanese banks have mostly finished dealing with the heavy load of bad loans inherited from the bursting of Japan's late 1980s "bubble" of soaring land and share prices. But smaller institutions still face problems.

Last week the Finance Ministry ordered a second-tier regional bank, Hanwa Bank Ltd, to halt most operations because the bank was unable to recover its bad loans and would no longer be able to operate as a going concern.
Tokyo share prices opened lower on technical sales, and brokers said the tankan data had little impact.
Japanese government bond futures, however, rose sharply as traders focused on the fact that big manufacturers and non-manufacturers both forecast a March diffusion index of minus one.
"The forecasts look pretty cautious...probably reflecting the anticipation of a consumption tax rise," said Peter Morgan, senior economist at James Capel Pacific.

Japan is set to raise its consumption tax, currently at three percent, to five percent from April 1. That, along with a possible end to special income tax cuts implemented for the past two years to keep the economic recovery on track, is expected to act as a drag on growth.
